candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'Azâzêl taught men to make swords, and knives, and shields, and breastplates' — the Watchers' second crime: teaching humans forbidden technologies that enable violence and seduction. The catalog continues with metallurgy, cosmetics, sorcery, astrology, weather magic, root-cutting, and astronomical secrets. The Tewahedo reading takes this as the prototype of every subsequent technology-corrupted-by-fallen-knowledge: the technologies themselves are not evil, but their introduction by rebel angels (rather than by the proper covenantal tradition) makes them weapons of disorder rather than tools of stewardship. This is the textual root of the Tewahedo monastic ascetic suspicion of certain technological luxuries.
candidates.reviewer_notes: Curated PD interpretive summary representing the Ethiopian Tewahedo tradition's reading via 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition), Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36). Verify the summary still reflects the source's argument before promoting; substitute a verbatim quote from the NPNF / Charles dump where available, and where applicable cross-check the Andəmta homiletic tradition for resonance.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And as men perished, they cried, and their cry went up to heaven' — the foundational text for the prayer-of-the-oppressed as cosmic-judicial appeal. The 'cry' (Geez 'awyāt) is involuntary lament of those suffering injustice; it ascends to heaven by divine ordinance, not by deliberate liturgical mediation. This is the textual basis for the Tewahedo doctrine of God's predisposition to hear the cry of the persecuted regardless of formal liturgical observance: oppression itself becomes prayer when borne by the innocent.
